notes:
Part of the paid AI for Research Workflows and Agents Certification, a 4-course programme. Read in a browser 2026-08-27, which is why `checked` moved.

THE CONTRADICTION IN THIS ENTRY IS THE SEMINAR'S OWN, not ours, and both of our fields were copied faithfully. Its page carries two sections that disagree:
  Who Should Register? - "you don't need any prior experience with AI tools or programming"
  Computing           - "You should be comfortable with basic LLM prompting and interaction and have a working knowledge of at least one statistical computing language (e.g., Python or R)"
`prerequisites` follows Computing, because that is the operative section: it is the one that tells you what to have installed and it is the stricter of the two. Neither was deleted, because deleting one would hide that the seller has not decided.

Also read off the page on 2026-08-27 and not previously recorded: the fee is $995 USD; it is 4 days on Zoom, 10:30-12:30 and 13:30-15:00 ET each day, roughly 14 hours, which is why `time` moved from half-day to multi-day; recordings appear within 24 hours and stay for four weeks; it needs a Claude Pro or Team subscription on top of the fee, and the page says a free-tier account is not recommended because of usage limits; 1 ECTS equivalent point; taught by Jeffrey Dotson.

`level` settled 2026-08-27, and it follows the same stricter section that `prerequisites` follows. This field is the reader's own Claude experience - the home page asks it as "I have never used Claude / used it a little / used it a lot / built things with it" - so it measures the entry bar and nothing else. The loose section ("no prior experience with AI tools") would make it never-used; the strict one ("comfortable with basic LLM prompting and interaction") makes it basic. It was `confident`, which neither section supports. The working knowledge of Python or R that the same sentence demands is a programming prerequisite, not a Claude level, and it is already recorded in `prerequisites` where a reader can see it.

skip_if: It is not about Claude. Not one instruction here is Claude-specific, and if you already have a prompting habit the CLEAR framework will not add to it. The ROBOT test is the part worth the visit: a checklist for evaluating a tool's own marketing, which almost nothing else in this catalogue offers.
teaches: structure a prompt with the CLEAR framework
evaluate an AI tool's claims with the ROBOT test
separate tool-specific skill from general AI literacy
questions: how do i judge whether an ai tool is any good
what is the clear framework
how should researchers think about ai

title: AI & Academic Integrity
author: Center for Teaching Innovation
summary: Cornell's guidance for instructors on AI and academic integrity: three model syllabus policies - prohibited, permitted with attribution, encouraged - then how to spot a violation, what counts as evidence, and how to cite AI output in APA, MLA and Chicago. About 3,000 words.
who_for: A teacher who has to write an AI line into a syllabus before term starts and would rather borrow three tested wordings than invent one.
skip_if: It is general generative AI, and its examples name ChatGPT rather than Claude. Read it for one thing above the others: it tells you not to lean on AI detectors, because they 'cannot provide evidence' for what they claim and testing has shown wide error margins. If your department is buying a detector, that sentence is the reason to read this page. No publication date is shown and some references are from 2023.
teaches: choose between prohibited, permitted-with-attribution and encouraged AI policies
gather evidence for a suspected violation without relying on detection software
cite AI-generated content in APA, MLA and Chicago
questions: what should my syllabus say about ai
do ai detectors work
how do students cite ai
